To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please talk to your kids this week — fake pills and calling 999

Parents, teenagers, anyone with mates going out: please read the police warning on here about fake blue tablets. And please share this, not just like it.

Blue pills are being sold as diazepam or “Xanax”. Some have been found to contain nitazenes — synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. You cannot tell what’s in a tablet by looking at it, or because someone says they’ve taken the same ones before.

I’m an ICU nurse, but this is general safety advice. I’m not commenting on what happened on Saturday, and I won’t be discussing anyone’s care. Please don’t name people or repeat rumours underneath this.

The bit I really want people to hear is this: if someone collapses, is difficult to wake, or isn’t breathing normally after taking something, ring 999 straight away.

Do not put them to bed to “sleep it off”. Do not leave them alone. Do not wait to see whether they’re better in an hour.

Warning signs include extreme drowsiness, pinpoint pupils — pupils that look unusually tiny — slow or noisy breathing, and blue lips. You don’t need to see every sign, know exactly what they’ve taken, or be certain it’s an overdose before calling.

Sometimes mates panic. They think getting someone into bed is looking after them, or they’re frightened of parents finding out or police turning up. But if someone’s breathing is slowing or stopping, their brain is being starved of oxygen. Waiting hours can mean help comes too late.

Tell the 999 call handler where you are and what’s happening. Say what they might have taken, if you know, and follow the instructions. If they’re unconscious but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position. If they’re not breathing normally, the call handler can guide you through CPR. Stay with them.

The police have literally said: “Our priority is preserving life.” Please let that sink in. Don’t let fear of getting in trouble stop you calling for help. Your mate needs you to make that call.

Nasal naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose, including one caused by nitazenes. It does not replace an ambulance: call 999 even if you give it and the person seems to improve. Use it according to the kit instructions; further doses may be needed.

Brightpath drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette, has free nasal naloxone kits. Anyone can ask, no names needed. Training takes about 10 minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday, 10–4, and Thursdays until 7. You don’t have to be someone who takes drugs to carry something that could save a life.

I had this chat with my lad, who’s 14, over his tea last night. Yes, there were eye rolls. But he listened, and he asked what pinpoint pupils meant. They do hear more than we sometimes think.

Please talk to your kids THIS week. Not after half term, not when they’re older, not once you think there’s a problem. Tell them they can ring you if they’re scared, and that if someone is unwell they ring 999 first.

And please stop slagging the kids off. You don’t have to approve of drug use to want someone to survive. Shame and threats make frightened kids less likely to ask for help. That’s exactly what we need to change.

Share the warning. Have the awkward conversation. Make sure they know: don’t put a mate to bed and hope. Ring 999.
